result:
The rain had been falling for three days, not the dramatic kind that floods streets and makes headlines, but a steady, thoughtful rain that turned the world the color of old pewter. In a small apartment above a bakery, someone sat at a wooden table with a notebook open and a cup of tea gone cold. They weren't waiting for inspiration so much as listening for it, the way you listen for a train you know is coming but can't yet see.

Outside, the gutters sang their thin metallic song. Inside, the only other sound was the occasional tick of the radiator. The person wrote a sentence, crossed it out, wrote another. Most of what appeared on the page would never be read by anyone else, and that was precisely why it mattered. There is a particular freedom in sentences that do not have to perform. They can wander. They can admit they don't know where they're going. They can stop mid-thought and simply notice the way the light changes when a cloud passes.

By evening the rain had thinned to a mist. The person closed the notebook without rereading what they'd written. Downstairs the bakery was locking its doors; the smell of tomorrow's bread was already beginning to rise through the floorboards. Somewhere in the notebook a half-finished line waited, patient as a seed. It did not need to become anything tonight. It only needed to exist long enough for the next quiet hour to find it.
